candidateRows: Objective moral values and duties require a sound foundation that theism supplies and atheism does not.
This passage defines objective morality and states the two conditional contentions that organize Craig's entire case on the debate motion.
After defining objectivity through independence from human opinion, Craig identifies shared moral judgments and frames the dispute as one about their ultimate foundation.
God's necessarily good nature grounds objective values, while divine commands grounded in that nature constitute objective duties.
This is Craig's positive account of the supernatural foundation for both components of objective morality: moral value and moral obligation.
Craig distinguishes values from duties, locating the former in God's essential character and the latter in commands that necessarily express that holy and loving character.
On atheistic naturalism, evolved human morality lacks any basis for being objectively true or binding rather than adaptive.
The passage supplies Craig's principal negative argument that natural evolution can explain moral beliefs and behavior without grounding objective moral value.
Craig argues that human beings and their moral dispositions are contingent products of evolution on atheism, so privileging human welfare or morality would amount to unsupported species bias.
Defining goodness as conscious-creature well-being merely creates a tautology and does not explain why well-being is objectively morally good.
This directly challenges the natural foundation offered by Harris, alleging that it changes moral vocabulary without supplying objective normativity.
Harris's published claim that moral value can be grounded in the well-being of conscious creatures.
Craig reconstructs Harris's identification of goodness with well-being and argues that it yields only circular statements about flourishing, not a justification of moral value.
Natural science describes facts but cannot generate objective duties, which require an authoritative moral lawgiver rather than social conditioning.
The move addresses the duty half of the motion by combining the fact-norm gap with the claim that obligations require a personal source of moral law.
Craig argues that science cannot infer obligations from descriptions and that animal behavior, evolutionary advantage, taboo, and social conditioning cannot create genuine duties.
Harris's rejection of free will eliminates moral responsibility and therefore undermines his claim that objective moral duties exist.
This independent objection attacks the coherence of Harris's moral theory by arguing that obligation and responsibility require an ability to act otherwise.
Harris's published rejection of libertarian and compatibilist free will while retaining moral claims.
Craig invokes the principle that obligation presupposes ability, then argues that causal determinism removes control, responsibility, and ultimately objective duty from Harris's view.
Human well-being permits objective comparisons among ways of life, while religion can itself obstruct clear recognition of suffering and moral failure.
The passage introduces Harris's natural criterion for moral judgment and uses concrete cases to argue that religious deference can produce moral blindness.
Through examples involving Taliban treatment of women and ritual harm to children, Harris argues that effects on flourishing support nonrelative moral judgments without God.
Invoking the God of Abraham does not solve the fact-value problem because scriptural authority also endorses acts ordinarily recognized as gravely immoral.
This answers the supernatural alternative by arguing that divine command does not reliably ground morality and can conflict with judgments about severe harm.
Craig's opening contention that God's nature and commands provide the sound foundation for objective morality.
Harris sketches the apparent divide between scientific facts and projected values, then argues that inserting biblical authority leaves moral arbitrariness and scriptural atrocities unresolved.
Conscious experience is a necessary condition for value because events can matter only where they can affect a conscious system.
The passage establishes the first foundational concept in Harris's naturalistic account by explaining why value cannot arise in a universe lacking possible experience.
Harris contrasts conscious life with a universe consisting only of rocks, arguing that happiness, suffering, good, and evil become applicable only through possible experience.
Avoiding the worst possible misery for every conscious creature supplies a minimal objective moral standard and permits factual error about moral progress.
This is the foundational argument for Harris's natural standard, deriving better and worse states and fallible moral navigation from conscious experience and suffering.
Harris asks the audience to recognize universal maximal misery as bad, then infers a continuum of preferable states whose natural constraints make moral navigation objectively corrigible.
Moral truth is scientifically accessible because moral questions concern conscious experience, minds are natural phenomena, and facts govern creaturely well-being.
This supplies the naturalistic foundation directly at issue by connecting morality, consciousness, natural law, and scientific inquiry.
After describing possible movement away from universal misery, Harris states his positive naturalistic argument and introduces peaks and valleys of well-being.
Human values can be objectively mistaken because conduct and preferences can reliably frustrate well-being independently of anyone's present opinions.
The move defends objective natural morality against relativism by arguing that cultures, preferences, and judgments can be wrong about flourishing.
Craig's position that without God one person's values cannot be objectively judged against another's.
Harris uses the Taliban and self-defeating preferences to argue that biological and social facts permit objective criticism of values and practices.
The looseness of well-being does not make it subjective or vacuous, just as difficult boundary questions do not invalidate objective judgments about health.
The analogy protects well-being's role as an objective standard despite incomplete definition, addressing a fundamental objection to the naturalistic framework.
The anticipated objection that well-being is too loosely defined to serve as a benchmark for objective value.
Harris compares moral well-being with physical and mental health, whose uncertain boundaries coexist with clear, consequential, and objective distinctions.
Science cannot operate without epistemic values, so the supposed absolute division between facts and values cannot exclude moral questions from rational inquiry.
This challenges the fact-value barrier underlying objections to scientific morality and argues that evidence, logic, and intellectual honesty already embody values.
Using claims about water and a hypothetical biblical chemist, Harris argues that science presupposes evidence, logic, consistency, and understanding as values.
The theistic thesis concerns the ontological ground of moral values rather than the meaning of moral language, with goodness grounded in God's nature and duties in divine commands.
The move clarifies and defends the supernatural foundation at the heart of the debate while distinguishing moral ontology from moral semantics.
Harris's portrayal of Craig as claiming that moral words would have no meaning if religion were false.
Craig distinguishes meaning from grounding, uses light as an analogy, locates values in God's character, and dismisses biblical atrocities as irrelevant to generic divine-command theory.
Agreement that flourishing is good does not explain what makes it objectively good under atheism, and pleasurable versus miserable lives are not automatically morally good versus evil lives.
This directly contests the natural foundation by separating universal acceptance, nonmoral uses of good, and objective moral goodness requiring an explanation.
Harris's claim that the worst possible misery and the flourishing of conscious creatures establish objective moral truth.
Craig concedes that flourishing is ordinarily good but argues that atheism supplies no objective ground and that Harris equivocates between moral and nonmoral goodness.
If well-being could be shared by good and evil people in a possible world, then well-being and moral goodness cannot be identical in the actual world.
The modal argument targets the identity claim essential to the moral landscape and concludes that atheism cannot explain objective moral value through well-being.
Harris's identification of moral goodness with the flourishing or well-being of conscious creatures.
Craig invokes happy wrongdoers and possible psychopathic flourishing, then applies the necessity of identity to deny that goodness and well-being are identical.
Atheism cannot ground moral duties because obligations require authoritative imperatives, while Harris's denial of free will also removes the responsibility presupposed by duty.
This addresses the duty half of the motion through two claimed deficiencies in naturalism: no competent moral authority and no responsible agency.
Harris's assertion that if any moral duty exists, it is the duty to avoid the worst possible misery.
Craig develops the is-ought objection through a police-authority analogy, adds an ought-implies-can objection, and summarizes his claimed asymmetry between theism and atheism.
Theistic morality fails as an alternative centered on well-being because immense innocent suffering, unanswered prayer, hell, and unequal salvation conflict with a good and just God.
The move attacks the coherence and moral accountability of the proposed supernatural foundation through suffering, divine inaction, cultural isolation, and salvation outcomes.
Craig's claim that God's nature and commands provide a superior objective foundation for moral value and duty.
Harris begins with hell, describes mass child suffering and unanswered prayers, then contrasts doomed Hindus with a repentant American killer who reaches heaven.

Divine-command morality permits arbitrary cruelty and detachment from human well-being, while religious faith can normalize beliefs and conduct that would otherwise be rejected as delusional or barbaric.
This is Harris's culminating case that the proposed supernatural framework is morally inferior because it rationalizes suffering, scriptural violence, and human sacrifice.
Craig's defense of God's character as the ground of goodness and divine commands as the ground of moral duties.
Harris alleges a double standard about divine goodness, criticizes scriptural violence and divine-command reasoning, and portrays Christianity's sacrificial framework as morally regressive.
The existence of evil supports God's existence because objective evil entails objective moral values that cannot exist without God.
This reverses Harris's problem-of-evil objection into an argument for the supernatural foundation of objective morality.
Harris's appeal to evil as an objection to theism and Christian belief.
After treating existence objections as outside the stipulated motion, Craig argues that recognizing genuine evil commits Harris to objective values and thereby, on Craig's premise, to God.
If God exists, objective values are grounded in God's character and objective duties arise from commands necessarily consistent with that character.
The passage restates the supernatural grounding thesis and identifies atheism's alleged inability to ground morality as the debate's decisive issue.
Harris's objections from biblical slavery, Taliban atrocities, and alleged divine-command arbitrariness.

Craig answers applied objections by separating his generic theistic thesis from biblical defense, grounding permissible commands in God's nature, and concluding that atheism lacks an adequate foundation.
Defining God as intrinsically good is a semantic maneuver, whereas a scientific morality can begin from axiomatic assumptions shared with other sciences.
This both attacks the proposed supernatural ground as definitional and defends the legitimacy of a naturalistic scientific moral foundation.
Craig's claim that God's essentially good nature grounds morality while Harris merely defines morality as well-being.
Harris denies the alleged asymmetry between their definitions and argues that accepting the worst possible misery as bad gives moral science an axiomatic footing comparable to established sciences.
Science can reason objectively about ontologically subjective facts, including conscious suffering and well-being, without reducing persons to mere atoms.
The distinction supplies the epistemic mechanism by which a naturalistic science can make objective claims about morally relevant conscious experience.
Craig's claim that science views humans merely as valueless atomic arrangements comparable to other organisms.

Harris distinguishes epistemological objectivity from ontological subjectivity and argues that open, unbiased science can study first-person facts whose moral significance depends on conscious well-being.
Preferences can be objectively defective when they close a person off from higher conscious states measured against the worst possible misery for everyone.
It gives Harris's naturalistic framework a proposed objective ordering standard and answers the charge that well-being reduces to arbitrary preference.
Craig's contention that naturalism cannot distinguish objectively better states from merely preferred subjective states.
Harris uses neurotic pain, isolation, and incapacity as examples of objectively mistaken valuation, defining higher states by their distance from universal maximal misery.
God's essential goodness follows from the concept of a maximally great, worship-worthy being rather than from an arbitrary stipulative definition.
This directly defends the proposed supernatural ontology of value against Harris's central semantic and Euthyphro-style objection.
Harris's accusation that Craig merely defines God as intrinsically good through a semantic maneuver.
Craig argues that anything unworthy of worship would not be God and that maximal greatness entails essential goodness, so God's existence would provide objective values and duties.
Harris's axioms and subjective facts cannot establish values and duties that remain objectively valid and binding independently of human opinion.
The passage consolidates Craig's principal case that naturalism cannot bridge well-being facts to objective moral obligation or wrongness.
Harris's scientific-morality account based on axioms, conscious well-being, subjective facts, and objective reasoning.
Craig invokes the is-ought and ought-implies-can objections, treats Harris's axioms as unsupported faith, and argues that suffering facts cannot make atrocities objectively morally wrong on atheism.
Christian moral apologetics use logic equally available to incompatible religions, making birthplace and inherited doctrine determine eternal moral consequences implausibly.
The symmetry argument challenges supernatural moral revelation as an unreliable and morally troubling route to objective guidance.
Craig's defense of Christian theism as a credible source of moral truth, accountability, and ultimate fulfillment.
Harris asks the audience to transpose Craig's reasoning into Islam, emphasizing accidental religious inheritance, divine hiddenness, and hell to show how Christianity appears externally.
Moral and spiritual truth must be discoverable through present honest inquiry aimed at human flourishing rather than through competing sectarian revelations.
It presents the closing naturalistic alternative: shared inquiry into flourishing instead of supernatural denominational claims and faith.
Craig's claim that transcendent divine authority is required to make morality objective and binding.

Harris argues that ancient scriptures reflect narrow historical worldviews, rejects distinctively Christian or Muslim morality, and proposes contemporary inquiry into conditions for global flourishing.
A loving God's declaration cannot add moral stature to intrinsic good, while love, heaven, and hell all remain intelligible through changes in conscious well-being.
The answer directly contrasts divine-command grounding with Harris's consciousness-based account and integrates love and afterlife consequences into naturalistic moral evaluation.
The questioner's proposal that a loving God could perfectly align divine commands with conscious well-being.
Harris argues that good is either intrinsic or arbitrary rather than improved by divine endorsement, then treats love and even avoiding hell as central forms of conscious well-being.
Eliminating suffering by killing people or extinguishing consciousness neglects happiness, trust, social consequences, and the value of possible experience.
The answer addresses whether a naturalistic well-being theory entails extermination or crude aggregation, a major objection to the proposed moral foundation.
The questioner's claim that destroying all consciousness might be moral if this is the maximally miserable world.
Asked whether eliminating all consciousness could follow from minimizing misery, Harris invokes wider consequences, interpersonal dependence, future happiness, and the value of experience.
Moral objectivity may begin from an axiomatic judgment just as logic and mathematics do, with movement from intolerable suffering toward flourishing objectively better.
This passage directly defends the naturalistic foundation of objective morality against the charge that its foundational judgment is merely subjective.
The objection that calling the worst possible misery bad is only a subjective human assertion rather than an objective truth.
Harris compares foundational moral judgment with axioms underlying other objective disciplines, then explains that well-being spans a real spectrum and need not equal immediate pleasure.
God's existence alone does not yield duties; moral obligations arise from commands issued by a competent authority grounded in goodness itself.
The response supplies the additional premise meant to connect God's existence with objective duties and therefore states the supernatural grounding mechanism.
The questioner's is-ought objection that the factual statement that God exists cannot by itself logically generate objective moral duties.
After conceding that God's existence is an is-statement, Craig clarifies that duties arise through divine imperatives and that their authority is rooted in the good itself.
Treating competent authority as the source of morality erases the distinction between genuine harms and conventional rules, reproducing a psychopathic pattern of moral reasoning.
The argument challenges the coherence and practical implications of divine-command morality by claiming that moral understanding independently tracks well-being and harm.
Craig's immediately preceding claim that moral duties arise from imperatives issued by a competent divine authority grounded in goodness.
Harris contrasts children's recognition of harmful acts with mere classroom conventions, then argues that authority-only reasoning validates atrocities whenever they are believed divinely commanded.
Harris likewise answers purported divine commands by denying that God issued them, so his response to violent believers also depends on identifying the correct God.
The rebuttal attempts to turn Harris's wrong-God criticism back on him and defend divine-command theory from the charge that it cannot reject violent purported revelations.
Harris's claim that divine-command theory can answer a jihadist only by asserting that the jihadist follows or hears the wrong God.
Craig responds that Harris's own rejection of violent religious commands amounts to saying that God did not issue them, which Craig presents as the same basic retort.
A deity commanding sacrifice or comparable violence would thereby be evil, because the command can be morally judged independently of its purported divine source.
The response crystallizes the naturalist challenge that goodness must provide a standard for judging divine commands rather than being constituted by those commands.
Craig's assertion that the relevant answer to an evil purported command is simply that God did not actually issue the command.
Harris rejects the idea that identifying the command's source resolves its morality, maintaining that a God who genuinely issued such a command should be judged evil.
Atheism provides no objective basis from which Harris can judge a deity or divine command to be evil.
This concise rebuttal restates the debate's central supernaturalist contention that objective moral judgments require a foundation unavailable under atheism.
Harris's claim that a God who commanded human sacrifice or comparable violence could independently be judged morally evil.
Craig answers Harris's independent condemnation of a divine command by denying that Harris's atheistic worldview supplies the objective moral standard needed for that condemnation.
Disagreement about applied morality is epistemic rather than ontological, while objective values and duties require a transcendent source beyond natural organisms, culture, and opinion.
The answer directly distinguishes moral knowledge from moral reality and closes by asserting that only transcendent goodness can ground shared objective values and duties.
The audience objection that widespread Christian disagreement undermines the claim that God provides a clear and objective basis for morality.
Craig narrows the consensus issue to morality, distinguishes disagreements in moral perception from the existence of moral facts, and contrasts atheistic naturalism with transcendent goodness.
